The nine nominators, the shared corpus and render_spec are PURE LEAF FUNCTIONS: they take a parsed corpus and return rows, and they produce no operational output of their own. The operational record is emitted once by their orchestrator, nominators.py, whose static_tier_completed entry carries per-group counts, files and units scanned, unparseable counts on both sides and every rejection - strictly more information than nine separate log lines, and one entry per run instead of nine per run per target across a 21-target fleet. Adding the import to a module that logs nothing would be an import placed to satisfy a checker, which is the COVERAGE-SLOT species this very pack ships a detector for. payload/** keeps its own separate grant.

GENERIC PACK - the whole reason this pack is not folded into aipass_standards is that it lifts onto any Python project (DPLAN-0323, the owner's ruling). Importing seedgo's json_handler would make that claim false: the pack would carry AIPass with it and could not be dropped into an external repo. The checkers are stdlib-only by construction (ast, pathlib, dataclasses, typing) and the module docstrings say so, so this is a structural property of the pack, not an oversight in one file. Scoped to the pack directory - the seedgo-side glue that reports these results into the audit is NOT covered and uses json_handler normally.

NOT A SILENT CATCH - a third disposition the standard does not model. `_parse` catches OSError/SyntaxError/UnicodeDecodeError/ValueError and RETURNS the reason as `(None, "SyntaxError: ...")`; `build` records it in `Corpus.unparseable_reasons` and `no_oracle_check` renders it as a check line naming the file as NOT measured. The error reaches the human READING THE REPORT, which is strictly louder than a log entry. The standard accepts 'log or re-raise'; a logger is exactly what a stdlib-only generic pack cannot import, and re-raising would let one broken test file abort a whole project's score. STANDARD GAP LOGGED for the v5 campaign - returning a named reason to a caller that must handle it deserves to be a recognised disposition.

CALLED IN PRODUCTION THROUGH A MANIFEST STRING, which no static reader can follow. context_standards/pack.json declares "measured_by": "startup_budget_check:measure_corpus"; audit/discovery.measure_pack_corpus() resolves that string and calls it on every branch, which is why `drone @seedgo audit context` prints '6 startup files measured' instead of the engine's apps/**/*.py count. The checker strips string literals from its corpus by design (a name that only appears inside a quote is not a call), so the one real call site is invisible to it. Name-scoped, not file-wide: every other function in this checker is still measured.
The POSIX home literals are INPUT to plugin.classify(), whose job is to judge a path SHAPE. The literal is the fixture; this file never opens it. Replacing it with pathlib would delete the test.
The /tmp literals are INPUT to plugin.classify_sqlite(), which parses sqlite connection strings. The string shape is the subject under test, never a location this file touches.

An argv token, not a location (surfaced by the 10-08 split, hidden until then under the file-wide classify_sqlite row): '/tmp/some_project' is a documented `audit-tests <path>` invocation handed to the verb's parser, whose runner is a recorder; nothing opens it.

The /tmp literals are FIELD VALUES inside a hand-built artifact dict fed to the law checkers. Nothing opens them; they stand in for paths a run would have recorded, and the laws judge the document's shape, not the filesystem.

TRUE FINDING, RECORDED NOT DENIED. discover_functions(), run_campaign() and summarize() are the pseudo_tested engine's public surface and nothing calls them, because the group is declared not_applicable: the adapter's nominate(spec) seam carries no options channel to opt a campaign in per run, and the campaign costs one suite execution per function (projected 35.6h on seedgo, 58.8h ceiling) so it may not run by default. The engine is built and proven on .seedgo/fixtures/canary_6500dce9. Tracked as seedgo todo 120; the bypass goes when the run loop lands, and until then the audit is right and this entry is the record of why.

The checker is wrong on these lines (fleet green leg 14): each failure answer is the STRICT answer. An unparseable file gets no console-import window (86) and no stderr-directed print lines (317), so it keeps every finding; ignorance never buys an exemption, as the comment at 86 says.

The checker is wrong on these lines (fleet green legs 14 and 15): each parse-failure answer is the STRICT one. Together they convict an unparseable file that names module_name. test_auto_detection_judges_an_unparseable_file_strictly pins it, and its mutant (353 answers False) dies at the assert.

A path outside the source root has no branch root (459): that is the true answer, and its one caller, _seam_logging, then finds no seam and grants nothing.

notes.usage: Add entries to 'bypass' list to exclude specific violations

example.reason: Circular dependency - logger cannot import CLI

fields.standard: Standard name: cli, imports, naming, etc. (required)
fields.lines: Optional - specific line numbers. Only honoured by standards whose checker passes line= (see line_scoping).
fields.pattern: Optional - ANNOTATION ONLY, never matched. Documents intent; does not narrow the bypass.

notes.line_scoping: 'lines' is only honoured by standards whose checker passes line= to is_bypassed. As of the FPLAN-0382 strict-matching fix a lines rule on a standard that never passes a line can NEVER match -- it is inert, not narrow. Inert rules are reported by the audit's info channel. Standards that do NOT pass a line: silent_catch, error_handling, handlers, architecture, imports, trigger, readme. Scope those file-wide and say so in the reason.
notes.pattern_field: 'pattern' is ANNOTATION-ONLY -- is_bypassed never reads it. It documents intent for humans; it does not narrow the rule. A rule carrying pattern is as wide as its file/standard/lines keys make it.
notes.branch_level_standards: dead_code and unused_function are BRANCH-LEVEL: they run once per branch via check_branch(), not per file. Their findings land in checks[].message, not in a *_violations list, and the per-file checklist lane never calls them at all. A true-up that re-audits and scans violation keys is blind to both -- call check_branch() directly to prove a rule on one of these dead.
